title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Forum
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Forum.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– You already know, Forum.
– Telepaths is on Vacation.
– Do you think they could help me?
– I don't know what's on your mind, robot, but Telepaths should.

The robot left, then realized he had forgotten to ask how to get to Vacation, and came back to Forum. When he returned, though, he found a Flame War. Suddenly Moderator appeared in the Thread, waving a Banhammer menacingly. The robot thought that a great many new characters had appeared while he was away.

– Everyone is going on Vacation!

And the robot went on Vacation with everyone else.
translatorNote: “Telepaths are on vacation” is a Russian forum reply to questions that leave out information readers would need to answer them.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Vacation
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Vacation.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– Have you come for a rest, robot?

The robot looked around. Good Weather walked past and sprawled unceremoniously in a deck chair, making it quite clear they had no intention of going anywhere for a long time. Out of the corner of his eye, the robot saw someone who looked like Ideas slip through the gate, as though trying to hide from someone.

– Actually, I'm looking for Telepaths.
– They're staying with me, robot.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Telepaths
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Telepaths.
– Why have you come, robot?
– Don't you know already?

The robot felt Telepaths' heavy gaze on him. It seemed his companion was scanning his thoughts and would soon have an answer.

– I'm on Vacation, robot.
– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Caravans
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Vikings.

Vikings was looking into the distance, where cows you could rob were walking in a neat queue. Somewhere beyond the horizon, little houses were spawning and elves were choosing themselves.

– I waited two whole years!
– I'm sad. In those two years, I still haven't found the Way.
translatorNote: The misspellings and odd game mechanics in the Russian refer to a much-quoted amateur proposal for an online game: “I waited two years” and “you could rob caravans.” Here the caravans have become cows.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and George Martin
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, George Martin.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.

Suddenly Vikings came round the corner and said:

– At last I meet my greatest rival face to face. Thank you for the tip, robot. George Martin, this world has no room for both of us.
– You're right, Vikings.

The writer's eyes flashed, and a crooked grin appeared on his face. Vikings took a fighting stance.

– Then let us settle this in a duel. Bearded man to bearded man.

George Martin drew a double-edged sword and engaged Vikings. Despite his build, the writer moved with the agility of a puma and was every bit the warrior's equal. His experience as a seasoned assassin and bloodthirsty killer was showing. George Martin made a sudden lunge at Vikings. Time, passing by, seemed to slow their step. The robot saw George Martin's sword pierce the warrior seafarer's chain mail and strike a fatal blow. Vikings fell to the ground and, looking into the robot's eyes, said with his last breath:

– Forgive me, robot. I've let you down. I've let everyone down...

The robot looked sadly at the fallen Vikings.

– I'm sad.

George Martin slowly and ominously withdrew his weapon, then set off in search of a new victim.
adaptationNote: The fatal wound is described with less anatomical detail; the duel and death are preserved.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Flying Philosophers
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Flying Philosophers.
– I know about your loss, robot. But I will put an end to George Martin's antics.

Twigs cracked. George Martin himself strode proudly out of the bushes. He was covered in blood, carrying the severed head of Shia LaBeouf in his left hand.

– Talking about me, are we?

Flying Philosophers attacked, but George Martin parried every blow with ease. Suddenly the writer pulled out a whip, apparently taken from Motivation, and struck Flying Philosophers with it. They split into Nietzsche and Camus, but both remained in the air.

– Nietzsche, you awaited the coming of the Overman! Here I am! I have rejected moral norms and forged my own worldview!
– You are a pathetic imitation, George Martin! And you will answer for your deeds!

Nietzsche rushed to attack. Metal clanged, and the robot saw a flash, as though lightning had passed between the opponents. A moment later they were both back where they had started. George Martin swayed a little, his glasses crooked and his cap knocked askew, but otherwise the writer seemed unharmed. Nietzsche hovered in the air with a stern expression. Suddenly a red stain appeared on his shirt over his heart. Camus saw his teacher's Fall, but reached him just in time to keep him from touching the ground.

– You must be strong, Camus.
– Don't leave me, teacher!

Nietzsche closed his eyes. Spread his fingers. And dissolved into hundreds of shining particles. The wind caught the philosopher's ashes and carried them into the sky. Nietzsche was dead.

– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Camus
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Camus.
– Robot, you must go. I probably can't defeat George Martin, but I can at least delay him.

Behind them came the writer's dreadful, thunderous footsteps.

– It seems it's just you and me now, Camus. As a gesture of goodwill, I will let you strike first.

George Martin spread his arms, leaving himself completely exposed. Camus summoned all his strength, created an enormous wave of absurdity, and sent it at his enemy. A dense existential fog engulfed the battlefield. The grass and bushes it struck became aware of their existence, understood its futility, and immediately crumbled to dust. When the fog cleared, the robot and Camus saw George Martin standing motionless, as though rooted to the ground. The writer's eyes were empty, as if he had looked into the Abyss.

– Now I see. How meaningless life and my existence are. It seems a midlife existential crisis has completely overtaken me.

Camus had decided it was over when George Martin suddenly broke into a wild grin and became the heartless killer he had been before.

– Fortunately, I stopped suffering from that nonsense long ago. I see my goal clearly, and I have no intention of retreating. Well, time to carry out the death sentence.

With those words George Martin was beside Camus in the blink of an eye, and ran him through. Looking at the philosopher's dead body, the robot said:

– I'm sad. He died a stranger after all.
translatorNote: “A stranger” alludes to Camus’s novel The Stranger; “the Fall” in the previous story likewise echoes a Camus title.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Caricature
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Caricature.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– I was made to amuse... you.

Caricature said the last word with a knife already in their back. George Martin had crept up unnoticed and committed another brazen murder. Suddenly President grew out of the asphalt and said:

– To prevent any further incidents of this kind, I am banning Tor.

Tor came out of the bushes. They smelled of onions.

– What have I done?
– You are clearly involved. There is no place for you in our society.

And with those words President killed Tor.

– Well? Did that help?

George Martin was holding his sword at President's throat. President instantly produced White Flag from behind their back. White Flag looked old and battered, as though they had been used more than once.

– I surrender, George Martin. Spare me.
– No one gets to steal my kills.

And with those words George Martin beheaded President.

The robot thought the murders were becoming rather frequent.

– I'm sad.
translatorNote: Tor is the anonymity network; its name and onion routing supply the onion joke.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Dead Hedge
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Dead Hedge. What happened to you?
– George Martin. As long as he continues his campaign, there will be more and more like me around here.
– I'm sad.
– Don't you have any ideas for stopping him, robot? Perhaps you could ask Taoist-Cocoaist for advice?
– I haven't seen them for a long time.

Suddenly a staff flew out of the Void and hit the robot in the back.

– Taoist-Cocoaist?
– I'm here.
– Where?
– Off-screen. George Martin can't get me here. Listen, robot. Whatever happens, keep following your Way.

Nearby came heavy footsteps and someone's grumbling. George Martin was dragging Creator along the ground, with a firm grip on his victim's hair. Creator looked battered and broken.

– You can torture me as much as you like, George Martin, but I've told you everything I know. I don't know who's behind all this, but it certainly isn't me. My business is building robots.
– You're simply useless.

George Martin roughly threw Creator down at Dead Hedge's roots. Creator coughed, straightened their glasses, and said:

– At least I have created something. All you can do is destroy!
– Only a talentless hack like you is content with the existing order, squeezing your creations into it. My plans are much grander. A true creator is free of obligations. To realize my vision, I will create a new world. But first I must destroy the old one.

With those words George Martin raised the axe he had taken from Vikings and delivered a fatal blow, beheading Creator at the robot's feet.

– I'm sad.

George Martin blew his nose into Dead Hedge, wiped his boots on Creator's body, and galloped off into Sunset.

– What do you think George Martin wanted to find out from Creator, robot?
– You're very talkative for a corpse, Dead Hedge.
adaptationNote: Creator’s death is preserved with less graphic description.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Sunset
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Sunset.

Sunset said something else, but the noise of Crowd drowned out their words. The robot decided to give his usual answer.

– I'm sad.
– I said, ever since George Martin began his bloody slaughter, everyone who couldn't fight has taken shelter here. But I'm not sure it's a good idea.

Suddenly there were footsteps as loud as thunder. Drooling, his boots creaking, George Martin stepped into the light.

– Quite the opposite. Now that you're all gathered here, I won't have to hunt you down one by one.

Crowd's murmur became a general wail. Then Jazz Leak stepped forward to face George Martin, white socks and polished saxophone gleaming. The writer met his opponent's gaze.

– Another defender? You're wearing me out.
– I'm not someone you can beat with brute force, George Martin. You won't touch anyone here. Over my dead body.
– Challenge accepted.

The saxophone uttered a complex polyphonic melody. Its dissonances burst into the masses of air and cut mercilessly through them. But the writer kept his head. In one quick movement he held a beautiful arch, and the destructive musical storm seemed not to touch him. This was only the beginning. The piece flowed into swing. Here too, George Martin was in his element. An elegant contraction danced him out of harm's way. In desperation, Jazz Leak began playing slap, but the peerless killer curved like a snake into a release and took the initiative completely. The atmosphere grew hot. It seemed flames were burning somewhere nearby. And they were! Dragons danced with George Martin, their fire consuming his opponents, while he, graceful as a lynx, set the heads of the fallen on stakes rising from the ground. A red haze and multicolored fire filled everything. More and more stakes appeared, like mushrooms after rain. Chaos triumphed. Then, to everyone's surprise, the writer threw his head back, raised one leg, and froze in that pose. It was over.

Jazz Leak had evaporated. George Martin wasn't even out of breath. It might have been a warm-up. He surveyed Crowd with a piercing gaze.

– Well, on to the rest.
– Wait!

A character in a dress stepped out of Crowd. The letter M in the middle bore Expert's unmistakable handwriting. The writer sighed in disappointment.

– When will you understand that I cannot be defeated?
– I don't intend to fight you, George Martin. It's pointless. I want to join your side.
– Who are you beneath that mask?
– I'm Marketing! I see your actions as a step into the New Future! And I want to share this moment of triumph with you!
– All right. Perhaps you'll be useful yet. For now, let us go on dancing!

And George Martin began to dance again. He beheaded everyone he met and deftly placed his trophies on the stakes. Sunset turned a deeper red than ever before. Eventually their turn came too. With a magnificent step, George Martin expertly sliced through Sunset with his sword, as smoothly and gracefully as though cutting silk.

Watching the Universe collapse, the robot said:

– I'm sad.
adaptationNote: The mass killings, dragon fire, beheadings, and trophies remain, while the repeated graphic blood imagery has been reduced.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Fourth Wall
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Fourth Wall. I hadn't noticed you before.
– I've always been here.

In the distance appeared Mongols, racing as fast as Wind. Soon they ran up to the robot.

– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Mongols. You're still alive?
– Praise Tengri! It was madness. Everyone ran. But while the others headed for Sunset, I went toward Sunrise, toward my native steppes. There's no way back! Nobody survived!
– Even Nobody? That's a pity. I never got to meet them. So what's your plan?
– I'll break through Fourth Wall, and we'll hide in the Beyond.
– But if there's a hole in the wall, George Martin can follow us through.
– That's exactly why I had the foresight to bring Chinese along. They can quickly rebuild walls after I've destroyed them.

Chinese stepped out from behind Mongols with a broad smile. The robot had never seen them before, but the smile looked familiar. Mongols took a running start and smashed through Fourth Wall. All three found themselves on the other side.

– Quick, Chinese, patch the hole.

But Chinese only giggled and took off their mask. Underneath was Marketing.

– You're so naive, Mongols. Now George Martin has a way into the Beyond.

George Martin's rapidly approaching figure appeared on the horizon. He wore new trainers and a bloodthirsty grin. Mongols galloped deeper into the new world, desperately throwing bricks at the oncoming threat. Looking at the laughing Marketing and the advancing George Martin, the robot said:

– I'm sad.
adaptationNote: An ethnic physical caricature has been removed; the characters, historical wall joke, disguise, and betrayal are preserved.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Readers
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello... who are you?
– Don't you recognize me, robot? I'm Readers. And I know you're sad.
– But how?
– I've been following your adventures for a long time. Lately, though, George Martin has somehow been getting all the attention.

The ground shook. Someone's mighty footsteps rumbled. The robot turned and saw George Martin advancing. Behind him, Marketing was barely keeping up on an exercise bike.

– So we meet at last, Readers.
– Go away, George Martin. I don't like you.

The writer ominously put his hands behind his back and, quite casually, produced two axes as though out of thin air. They bore the marks of many brave heroes and defenseless victims. Marketing leapt from their vehicle.

– Wait, George Martin. Are you going to kill Readers?
– Yes. They're a relic of the old order.
– But isn't all of this for their sake?
– You've misunderstood something, Marketing. The sole purpose of my murders is to raise myself above everyone else!
– That's not what I pedaled all this way for!

Suddenly a formidable voice filled Space like rolling thunder. The surrounding space warped and changed beyond recognition. Where there had been a half-ruined world, with a gaping void in place of Sunset, there now stood an actual arena. Marketing tore off their mask. Underneath was Paladin. Polished armor gleaming, an enormous hammer in their hands, they stepped between George Martin and Readers.

– There's more to you than I thought, Marketing.

George Martin took a fighting stance and bared his teeth. The battle of the two giants began. Their stamping shook the ground, and the clash of metal battered the air for miles. The sparks from each meeting of axe and hammer shone so brightly that Readers had to put on sunglasses. Paladin seemed invulnerable. Even when the writer caught the hero with an axe, the blade could not pierce the warrior's strong armor. George Martin, in turn, nimbly dodged the hammer. Readers watched the battle in admiration. They had never imagined their fate would be in Marketing's hands.

Paladin's radiance reflected from Readers' glasses and blinded George Martin for an instant. Marketing seized the moment and struck the enemy's head squarely with the hammer. The writer's glasses cracked; the blow bloodied his mouth and cost him several teeth. Paladin prepared another strike, but the writer deftly sprang away at the last moment. He stood to his full height, showing his enraged, battered face. George Martin went berserk and delivered one furious blow after another. His clothes could not withstand such speed and tore to shreds. With every blow, great dents appeared here and there in Paladin's armor. At some point the armor began to split. Without losing a second, George Martin swung at his opponent's neck with all his might, trying to behead Marketing in a single blow. The hero leaned on their hammer to keep from falling. Paladin wanted to look into Readers' eyes, but Readers was wearing sunglasses. The writer, his mouth bloodied, leaned toward his opponent.

– You're the only one who has put up a worthy fight, Marketing. Out of respect for a warrior as strong as you, I will spare Readers.

And George Martin struck the final blow. Marketing died with a smile on their face.

– I'm sad.
adaptationNote: The battle, wounds, lost teeth, attempted beheading, and death are preserved; graphic descriptions of blood have been softened.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Authors
text:
– Robot? What are you doing here?
– Hello, Authors. I came through the hole in Fourth Wall.
– Can the others come here too?
– The few who are still alive can, yes.
– But that means...

Gold teeth flashing, belching fire without restraint, George Martin entered the chambers.

– Well, hello, Authors.
– George Martin, you're not allowed in here. Disappear!
– You of all people should know words alone aren't enough to make someone really disappear. If you want to be good at your craft, you must build up the plot gradually before removing an important character.
– I'll destroy you, George Martin!
– With whose hands? All your warriors, whom you so diligently sent after me, died weaklings' deaths. Only Marketing put up a worthy fight. And you weren't even fond of them. How ironic.
– That's not all. I have an ace up my sleeve.

Authors waved a hand, and PR Manager appeared in front of George Martin, sword at the ready. The writer studied his opponent.

– I was wondering where you'd got to. Your friend Marketing saved Readers at the cost of their own life. But don't think I'll spare Authors, even if you prove a worthy opponent.
– Enough talk, George Martin. Combat will decide everything.

PR Manager held out their blade, inviting the writer to a duel. George Martin drew his own weapon and took a fighting stance. The battle that followed was so epic and spectacular that Authors would never have had the talent or money to animate it properly. Neither fighter gave ground. Both fought calmly, deftly parrying the other's blows. At one point, however, a blade brushed PR Manager's pretty face. They jumped back, holding their wounded cheek.

– Losing your touch, PR Manager?
– It seems I let my guard down. It won't happen again.

And PR Manager rejoined the fight with renewed strength. Suddenly one of George Martin's suit buttons caught on Space. PR Manager wasted no time exploiting the enemy's brief confusion. Their sword ran the writer through. The old man groaned and coughed blood. PR Manager was already anticipating victory, but George Martin continued to advance despite his wound. He moved closer and closer along the blade, until it reached its hilt. PR Manager seemed petrified, staring in horror at the unshakable opponent. The writer came right up to them.

– Not bad. Not bad. But not enough.

With those words George Martin beheaded his opponent. PR Manager had fallen. Leaving the sword where it was, the writer turned to Authors.

– Time to say goodbye.

With an inhuman leap, George Martin drove his sword into Authors' heart. Authors gave a faint cry and fell to the floor.

– Very soon, everything will change. There is only one more level to overcome.

With a sickly giggle, the insatiable killer moved Authors' lifeless body aside and headed deeper into the chambers.

– I'm sad.
adaptationNote: The sword wound and deaths are preserved with less anatomical and graphic detail.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Canons
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Canons.
– Do you have anything to say, robot?
– I think George Martin will be here soon.
– Let him come. I'm in no danger. I cannot be broken.

George Martin's heavy footsteps echoed down the corridor. Soon the bloodthirsty killer entered the hall. He still bore the wound PR Manager had given him, but the writer paid it no attention at all.

– At last I've found you, Canons.
– Why have you come?
– I have come to destroy the foundation of all foundations. You.

George Martin swiftly drew his sword and swung it at Canons. The blade shattered. Only the hilt remained in the attacker's hands, and the unexpectedly strong recoil threw the writer into a wall.

– Your weapon is nothing against me.
– Well, it seems this time I'll have to use my head.

And George Martin went to the library. There the writer pored over ancient tomes for three days and three nights in a row.
He returned with a sack over his shoulder.

– Back again?
– But this time with a surprise.

Pinkie Pie shot out of the sack like a cannonball, accompanied by confetti.

– Hello, Pinkie Pie.
– Ooh, hi there! How are our Canons doing?

Hairline cracks began appearing in Canons.

– You must say “How is our Canons doing,” Pinkie Pie.
– I thought I could say whatever I liked.

The cracks became visible to the naked eye.

– You must use the masculine form of “thought,” Pinkie Pie.
– Okey-dokey. Anything for the Canons.

The cracks kept growing.

– Look, George. I think something's wrong with the Canons.
– Sometimes your head is the strongest weapon.

Breaks and fissures appeared here and there. Then George Martin took a run-up and charged headfirst into the very heart of Canons. Canons broke into hundreds of shards. One fell at the robot's feet. Written on it were the words “And the robot is still sad.”
adaptationNote: The existing injury is described without graphic anatomical detail.
translatorNote: The Russian canon makes every named interlocutor grammatically masculine and singular, even a plural name such as Canons. Pinkie Pie breaks those grammar rules by using plural agreement and a feminine past-tense verb. English does not mark the speaker’s gender on “thought,” so that correction is made explicit.

title: George Martin's Monologues
text:
Throughout my career, I have killed characters. I don't know. Perhaps I'm just a bloodthirsty bastard. But it's so much fun.

---

There is no democracy in art. People cannot vote for the ending they like. All power is in my hands!

---

If the plot needs a turn, there's nothing wrong with introducing a character who will make it happen. Once that duty is done, the hero can peacefully die. An agonizing death.

---

From now on, I'm in charge here! And my word is law! A new order and new canons! Nothing can stop me!

title: George Martin Who Kills and Morgan Freeman
text:
Belching flames and shuffling his boots, George Martin danced on the ashes of the old world order. Canons had been destroyed. Authors was dead. A north wind howled over Marketing's grave. Though since Sunset's death, telling the directions apart had become harder. Readers refused to accept what had happened. After a funeral tap dance, George Martin stopped sharply, his glasses flashing.

– Well, the main obstacles are behind me. Now I make the laws of this world.
– But how did it happen? Why has the world changed so much?

Readers was bewildered. Suddenly Morgan Freeman emerged from the darkness, freckles shining, scratching his gray beard. He sat in a comfortable chair and began his account.

– You see, all this time George Martin had been moving steadily toward his goal: rising above everyone else. But he did not immediately understand how to achieve it. George Martin tried to get the necessary information out of the Creator of the Robot Who Is Sad. When he saw that Creator knew nothing, he concluded that there was some higher power. Having secured Marketing's support and tricked Mongols into using their ability to break through walls, George Martin reached the upper level of existence. There he could get at Authors, who guarded Canons. Having overcome the last line of defense, he destroyed Canons too, removing the final obstacle. New laws were needed. Taking the opportunity and using his literary talent, George Martin established his own world order and displaced the Robot Who Is Sad as Main Character.

Readers listened intently to Morgan Freeman's intelligent voice.

– If it was all about the Robot Who Is Sad, why didn't George Martin simply kill him?
– That's a very good question, but the answer is simple. George Martin knew that without the Robot Who Is Sad, everything would stop, because Canons required his presence. That is, he could not get rid of the robot before Canons had been destroyed. And now there's no need to do it at all.
– You're so good at explaining things, Morgan Freeman.

Readers began to clap. Morgan Freeman smiled beneath his mustache. A new freckle gleamed on his face.

A thunderous cough was heard. George Martin once again claimed everyone's attention.

– You've missed something, Morgan Freeman. The new Canons have already been written, and they say someone must die by my hand every time a dialogue begins.
– Yes. And today I will sacrifice myself to postpone the others' fate. But I will fight you. That's what you wanted, isn't it, George Martin? A world of battles in which you always win? It wouldn't be fair to your vision if everyone simply gave up.
– As perceptive as ever, Morgan Freeman.

They hurled themselves at one another. Morgan Freeman wore his ever-present smile; George Martin, a serial killer's snarl. Naturally the writer, with more experience of battle, had the advantage. Watching such an unequal fight brought tears to Readers' eyes. At last George Martin's sword caught Morgan Freeman. Readers' tears began falling to the ground. In every drop was the actor's encouraging smile, offering hope that someday everything would return to the way it had been.

title: George Martin's Canons
text:
1. Every dialogue has a title of the form “George Martin Who Kills and {interlocutor},” where {interlocutor} is replaced by the next victim.
2. The interlocutor may be absolutely anyone or anything, including an inanimate being or an idea. George Martin doesn't care who he kills. The interlocutor's name may consist of several words in any language, or numbers, but it always begins with a capital letter, except names beginning with a digit. Names must not be shortened in dialogue, except when the interlocutor is the peerless George Martin Who Kills. Then “George Martin” is permitted, provided you show him respect, wretch!
3. Turn around. George Martin may be behind you. And naked.
4. George Martin is God. And God's words and actions are above all canons.
5. In every dialogue, George Martin kills at least one character. George Martin is immortal. The victim need not be named in the title of the dialogue, though they will not escape their fate either way.
6. When you are alone with yourself, recall the great deeds of George Marin.
7. George Martin is still killing.
translatorNote: “George Marin” in rule 6 preserves the original’s spelling slip.

title: George Martin Who Kills and Robert McKee
text:
As usual, George Martin sat on his iron throne, contemplating the pile of skulls before him. The light of the dead Sun fell through slits in the stone walls of the writer's fortress and played over the yellowed bones. The fantasy author's gaze was full of fire and resolve. He was preparing another bloody expedition for new trophies. His faithful blade, honed to perfection, tickled his mighty hand with a pleasant chill. Everything froze in ominous silence, preparing to meet a terrible storm.
The silence was broken by a fantastic whirlwind, drawing all existence into itself. It was an explosion of literary emanations that only one man could command: Robert McKee. At that very moment, he burst into the great writer's dwelling.

– I'll teach you a lesson or two!
– You?! – George Martin chuckled. – You're pathetic, Robert McKee! All you can do is talk about things you know nothing about! While I build a new world with my own hands!
– You're not the hero of this story! And you're not its author! Good always defeats evil! And soon you'll see it!

Horrible laughter filled the corridor. The walls shook, and the ceiling began to crumble.

– Authors has been dead for ages! And now I have the leading role! Nothing can stop me, least of all a failure like you!
– Your kind never become protagonists!
– We'll see about that!

With the grace of a snake, George Martin leapt several meters forward from his throne and landed in a fighting stance. His opponent kept his composure. Straightening his kilt, he drew his enormous, furious axe, shining in the spotlight. Fire flashed in the eyes of both opponents, ready to fight to their last breath.
The writer struck again and again, forcing his rival onto the defensive. The onslaught was relentless, but Robert McKee had no intention of giving up. Parrying another thrust at his honor, he breathed fire straight into George Martin's face. Smelling the toxic fumes of whisky on his breath, the novelist retreated, giving his opponent time for another trick. With a sharp, deft movement, he split his axe in two, preparing to unleash a storm of steel. With a wild cry, like an untamed squid that had caught its prey, the warrior in the kilt rushed his rival. But George Martin could not be taken by surprise. Seasoned by years of combat, the writer easily blocked his opponent's clumsy maneuver and knocked him to the ground with a spinning kick.

– You may think you're strong, but true skill only comes in battle! – With those words, George Martin ran the body before him through.

title: George Martin Who Kills and Pet Shark
text:
Enjoying his newfound fame, George Martin lovingly stroked his beard. The feeling of unlimited power wrapped warmly around his mighty body. Incredible plans for arranging this little world raced through his mind. He spent long hours considering its ideal topography: where seas of blood would spread, and where mountains of bones would pierce Sunset's lifeless body. But his luscious dreams were interrupted by a light prickling at his neck. Turning one eye toward the source of the impertinent disturbance, George Martin discovered a hammerhead shark with its teeth in his neck.

– What sort of games are these?
– I'm here to stop you!

A sturdy man in water skis parachuted down in front of the writer. He wore a leather jacket, which he immediately took off, and held a shark in his hands. Smiling broadly, the stranger aimed the shark at the fantasy author. The master of pen and axe gave his guest an indifferent look and declared in a booming voice:

– I don't care who you are. You're going to die.
– I fear nothing but fear itself!

With those words he pulled the fish's fin. Jet-powered sharks with fists for heads began flying out of its toothy mouth. But George Martin's reflexes were as good as ever. Pausing for a second in an arabesque, he gracefully jumped over a shark flying toward him. It produced a mushroom cloud behind his back. Still airborne, he sharply pulled off the hammerhead shark and, using it as a weapon, descended on his opponent in a furious whirlwind.
His opponent kept his head. He was prepared for this turn of events and, with little difficulty, jumped over the shark too. The water-skier had done that trick before. But by the time he landed, George Martin was already behind him.

– And there go your happy days.

With those words, the writer broke his attacker's neck.
adaptationNote: The shark bite is described without specifying an artery.
translatorNote: The water skis, leather jacket, “happy days,” and repeated shark jumps allude to the scene that gave rise to “jumping the shark.”

title: George Martin Who Kills and Tyrion
text:
George Martin strode through the world with a deadly tread. Like a plague, he left mountains of corpses and broken hopes in his wake. The moment anyone came into his sight, the countdown to another bloody killing began. Everyone scattered and hid as best they could, leaving their homelands and homes. No one wanted to meet their own death face to face. But a legend said that somewhere in distant lands, a true hero was carousing in taverns and enjoying the brothels. The only one George Martin could not kill.

Learning of the world's fate, this great warrior decided to show his true nature. Within his body lived no small, miserable soul cowering in a corner, but a giant's soul: a great man with a great heart. Draining the last mug of his swill, Tyrion set off. Toward an unequal battle.

The writer continued his bloody march. He liked his new position as creator. There were so many beautiful deaths and so much splendid suffering in the world he had made. And there would be more. Now nobody could stop him for certain. Suddenly, though, a small figure appeared before him.

– Do you really think you can simply kill everyone? You're a creator. You ought to understand that an empty world won't keep you entertained for long.
– You?! How dare you come here and stand in my way?! You're nothing but my slave.
– I'm beyond your power. You may call yourself creator or God as much as you please. But as long as my head is still on my shoulders, it alone decides my next step.
– Then I'll simply remove it!
– I don't think it will be that easy, George Martin. This fight will be hard for you.
– You're forgetting something, Imp. I'm not yours to toy with.

With those words George Martin rushed Tyrion, his sword raised high above his head. Without losing a second, Tyrion slid deftly between the writer's legs. Drawing a dagger from his belt, he slashed his opponent's calves. Howling like a savage tiger, the novelist turned and took a broad swing at his rival's head. Tyrion could not avoid the swift blow entirely. Though he rolled aside, it still caught his shoulder. At that very moment, the same wound appeared on the writer's shoulder. Taken by surprise, the fantasy author cried out.

– Now you see, – said the Imp, holding his wounded shoulder. – By killing me, you'll hurt yourself too. You cannot be a creator through destruction alone.
– Then let's see which of us lasts longer.

With a growl, the writer hurled himself at his enemy and pierced his heart. Both fell silent, their eyes clouding. They stood motionless in that fatal embrace, like two lifeless statues.

A minute later, though, the professional killer came to. He slowly pushed Tyrion away to free his sword. Mumbling something like “Don't think sentimentality can stand in my way,” he continued on toward more battles.
adaptationNote: A sexual insult has become a defiant threat. Disability-based labels are replaced by Tyrion’s name, while his established epithet “the Imp” remains. Graphic wound details are reduced; the battle, mirrored injuries, and death are preserved.

title: George Martin Who Kills and All-Knowing One
text:
Towering over the remains of his many victims, George Martin gazed into the distance at Sunset's corpse. Suddenly, clothes rustling, All-Knowing One stepped out of the shadows and stood behind the novelist. They wore sunglasses, a leather hat, and Onotole's Vest. Without turning toward his opponent, George Martin said:

– Finally decided to come into the light? I've been waiting for you.
– For too long I was merely an observer. Now you've gone so far. I cannot stand aside.
– Decided to intervene?

The killer's voice became uneven, his body trembling a little. But the battle-hardened writer was overcome by excitement at the prospect of an interesting fight, not fear. At last the novelist turned to his opponent, treating the audience to a bloodthirsty grin. All-Knowing One smiled almost imperceptibly and slowly removed their hat, revealing a bald head so dazzlingly shiny that George Martin had to rub his eyes. The reason for wearing dark glasses became clear. But All-Knowing One soon removed those too. Beneath the sunglasses were ordinary glasses. Then Readers recognized Onotole himself in All-Knowing One. He raised his eyes, filled with knowledge, toward the writer waiting in his fighting stance.

– I declare in plain language: your atrocities end here!

And the intellectual giants met face to face: beard against beard, glasses against glasses. The very earth shook beneath both opponents' intellectual weight. Unable to withstand the intensity of battle, a volcano awoke in the distance, and a tsunami began approaching from the ocean. The fantasy author moved quickly and forcefully, but with caution. Noticing this, All-Knowing One said:

– I've worked out your plan, George Martin. You're afraid of damaging Onotole's Vest because you want it for yourself.
– I see the rumors of your wisdom were not exaggerated. But don't think I can't deal with you. Canons is on my side.

Onotole only smiled mockingly in reply and continued the fight. George Martin aimed at the legs and head, but somehow, as though foreseeing every move the novelist made, the sage avoided his blows. At one point the writer did have a chance to take his opponent's head off. Just before the blow, though, Onotole's Vest turned up its collar. The experienced warrior stopped his weapon a moment before it touched the coveted garment. Taking advantage of the fantasy author's confusion, Onotole kicked him with all his might. George Martin flew backward, and the sword fell from the insatiable killer's hands. All-Knowing One caught up with his opponent and leaned over him with a mustached smile.

– Your reign won't last long.
– Rubbish!

George Martin's confident shout swept across the decaying lands. Smoke from the erupting volcano filled the space. All-Knowing One's glasses became sooty. In one sharp movement, the writer grabbed his rival by the beard and, with a titanic effort, threw him over himself. The crash of Onotole's fall carried for miles. The earth opened beneath the sage, and he fell toward the boiling lava. Just before he plunged into the flames, Onotole's Vest broke free of its owner and escaped the fissure, carried upward by hot air.

Seeing his coveted prize, George Martin began taking off his outer clothes. Onotole's Vest shrank back, preparing for its fate. The novelist picked it up from the ground and forced his prize onto his sweaty body, merging with the garment into a single whole. Onotole's Vest recognized a new master. All of All-Knowing One's wisdom, accumulated over long years of observation, now belonged to the writer.

title: George Martin Who Kills and Deus Ex Machina
text:
George Martin followed the trail of his next victim with confidence. In the new world, engulfed in fire, fewer and fewer potential targets remained. Defenders no longer sprang from every corner, and every survivor knew the only chance was to run without looking back. But the writer had once been a professional tracker. A real hunt only heightened his excitement.

His experienced nose caught the smell of rust. With a cheetah's grace, the predator raced toward his prey. Tearing vines with his teeth and uprooting trees that dared stand in his way, the novelist rushed toward his goal. Soon his sharp eye caught the robot's silhouette.

– So we meet at last, Robot Who Is Sad! How do you like your new feeling: fear?
– I'm sad.

Suddenly space warped. A smoking rift appeared between the robot and the writer, spilling buckwheat and the sound of eighties synth-pop. A hand emerged from the hole, clutching a bold-looking car. The car door opened, and someone trustworthy stepped out. Taking a heroic stance, they said in a cool voice:

– I'm here to save the day.
– Who are you?! How dare you stand in my way?!
– I'm Deus Ex Machina. Today I'm your opponent.
– Deus Ex Machina? Have those hacks really become that desperate? Whoever you are, I'll simply kill you.

George Martin's whole mighty body was ready to leap, but something stopped him. Onotole's Vest tightened, clinging to its new master with every thread and every stitch, binding his movements.

– Listen, robot, – Deus Ex Machina began. – You'll only have one chance. I can give you one more dialogue.
– What are you talking about?! – the writer shouted, still fighting his unruly clothes. – That would contradict the canons!
– There's a loophole. But your pride has blinded you. Even the wisdom of the Universe didn't help you see your own mistake. – They turned back to the robot. – But this dialogue is our last hope. You must decide who it will be with. Who can help save the world. But... – Deus Ex Machina paused. – I must ask you something. Are you sure you want to change everything? The old Canons is gone, and you are no longer bound by sadness.

The recent events flashed through the robot's mind. He had lost so many close friends. All had fallen to George Martin's dirty paws. Even Marketing, the brave knight in shining armor.

– Perhaps I can feel anything now. But the only thing I feel is sadness.
– Then it's decided, robot! By the power of God vested in me, I grant you a new dialogue! All our fates are in your hands!

The writer finally broke free of the Vest and tried to tear it to pieces, but it flew into the sky, fluttering its many pockets. Deus Ex Machina picked up the robot and flung him to the far side of the world. They looked at the fantasy author and said coldly:

– Now I'm ready to accept my fate...
translatorNote: Deus ex machina means a device that resolves a plot through an unexpected outside intervention. The name’s “Deux” spelling at its first appearance in the original is normalized here.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Selfie
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Selfie.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– That's because you don't spend enough time with me.
– What would be the point?
– You need to take a selfie every day so you can fix Past if something happens.
– Selfie, can you do that?
– Not quite. But if you concentrate on me very carefully, you can go back to Past.

The robot strained every circuit, staring into Selfie. Suddenly Space began to shrivel, and Time stepped backward, taking the robot along.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Past
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Past.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.

The robot found himself in front of Carpet, holding Phone, just as on the day he had taken his first and only selfie.

– Robot, are you all right?
– I'm sad, Carpet.

The robot hurriedly left his companions. Carpet exchanged a look with Phone and merely shrugged their fibers.

The robot ran without knowing where. Suddenly he collided with Vikings' mighty body.

– What's the hurry, friend?
– Vikings, you're alive.
– Of course I'm alive. What did you think?
– I've come from a future where George Martin began killing everyone, then took power over the world.
– What are you talking about, robot? Been drinking with Spider again?
– He killed you too, Vikings.
– Stop making things up. If I met that old man, I'd chop him down with my axe.
– No, Vikings. If you meet George Martin, don't fight him. Run. You cannot defeat an enemy like that. I've seen his power.
– Me, a mighty warrior, defeated by some pathetic writer?

But the robot was already running on, looking for a sage who could help prevent the dark future.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Onotole's Vest
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Onotole's Vest.
– You look sadder than usual. What's troubling you?
– Where is Onotole himself? I need his wisdom.
– Why do you think I'm on my own? My owner is in the bath. Best not disturb him.
– I'm sad.
– But I'll try to answer your question. Onotole and I share each other's wisdom.

The robot told Onotole's Vest about the events of the future and the deaths that had befallen the various characters.

– That's a complicated story, robot. I don't know how to prevent those disasters. But since Death is involved, I suggest you speak to someone who's on the same foot as that fellow. Terry Pratchett.

As soon as he heard the name he needed, the robot left Onotole's Vest.
translatorNote: “On the same foot” preserves the original’s altered form of the Russian idiom for being on equal terms; the usual idiom has a “short,” or familiar, foot.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Terry Pratchett
text:
– Hello, Terry Pratchett.
– Hello, robot. I've been expecting you. How are you feeling?
– I'm sad.
– I'm sorry to hear that... Sit down and make yourself at home.

The robot entered a spacious but modest house. Everything inside gave off warmth and comfort. Passing enormous bookcases, he sat at a cream-colored coffee table. A suspiciously ancient-looking turtle flew past and waved a friendly flipper. Meanwhile the welcoming host immediately set a little cup of fragrant green tea before his guest.

– You're too kind for a writer.
– Or you've been unlucky with my colleague. So what brings you here?
– I need to meet Death.
– Don't go looking for Death. It's a waste of time. He'll find you when he needs you.

There was a knock at the door. Terry Pratchett left.

– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Time Who Has Come
text:
– Lao Tzu! Time Who Has Come! Good to see you!
– Hello, Terry Pratchett. Well? Ready for a board-game marathon?
– Of course. Only I have another guest at the moment.

The three of them went into the sitting room, where the robot sat alone, looking at his untouched tea. The turtle, deciding to get some fresh air, flew out through the little window.

– Hello, robot! Have you found the Tao?
– Hello, Lao Tzu. I tried, but Time refused to come.
– But now I'm here.
– So this is the end of the Way? All this time Taoist-Cocoaist was leading me in the right direction...
– Taoist-Cocoaist?!

Lao Tzu sighed and rolled his eyes. A fierce desire to fulfill his duty flared within him, despite his pressing business. He went up to the robot and laid his palm on his forehead.

– All right, robot. There's something I must show you.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and the Taoist's True Nature
text:
Space rushed away at incredible speed. Cupboards, tables, and other furniture crumpled like modeling clay, stretching into thin sausages and shooting upward. Everything around became an uneven multicolored mass. Lao Tzu floated beside the robot in that chaotic ether.
– What's happening?
– You need to meet Taoist-Cocoaist's True Nature. It will explain a great deal.
At the end of their flight, the travelers found themselves in an old, lifeless little village. A modest scattering of houses looked forlorn, inspiring only hopelessness. The sparse vegetation, yellow and withered, drooped. Beneath the pagoda of a decrepit, half-ruined house with rotten black walls sat an unremarkable old man, wrapped in dirty rags. The sage pointed toward him, but the robot was still puzzled.

– Who is that?
– One of my followers. Like everyone else, he sought the Way, but lost it.

The sky darkened to purple. Large drops of a thick black liquid began falling to the earth. A strong, slightly bitter smell of chocolate and nutmeg rose. The old man barely stirred and looked up at the sky. His face filled with the deepest reverence, as though he had seen the sign he had awaited all his life.

As soon as it hit the ground, the black liquid began to move. As though obeying a single will, its tiny particles all made for a point only a few steps from the old man in rags. Reaching their destination, the drops expressed their profound contempt for gravity and climbed over those already there. Soon the structure made from the black substance began to resemble a human figure. A long, thin human figure made of cocoa.

Taking an uncertain step forward, the creature raised its arms to the sky. The old man leapt up and walked toward the strange being. Reaching it, he froze. The dark figure pierced him with its long, spear-like arms and began pulling itself into his living body. A few moments later, neither the old man nor the creature was there. Only Taoist-Cocoaist stood in the empty village.

– ?
– Don't play with Eastern Philosophy, robot. It's too complicated and dangerous for you.

Having said this, Lao Tzu bounded up the bamboo stems into the sky. The vision evaporated, leaving the robot alone in the middle of an endless desert.

– I'm sad.
adaptationNote: The creature’s bodily invasion is preserved, while blood and anatomical wound details are reduced.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Cunning Plan
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Cunning Plan.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm... You know what? To the Abyss with everyone. The two of us can manage.
– What do you want to do?
– Stop George Martin. Once and for all. I may have turned Time back, but unless something changes, everything will happen again.
– But that's not your only problem, is it?
– True. There's Taoist-Cocoaist too. If they set me on the Way again, my hands will be tied. How can I get two birds with one stone...

The robot and Cunning Plan began brainstorming, loudly discussing their ideas. So many details had to be accounted for, so everything would form a single picture, every card would play properly, and the perfect game of solitaire would come together. At some point the robot saw the light.

– Of course. Once George Martin begins killing, he'll destroy everything he sees. All that's left is to get those two in one place.
– And how will you lure George Martin there?
– That will be easy. He could never resist killing Sean Bean.
– Sounds like a good idea. What about Taoist-Cocoaist?
– Sean Bean? Where did you come from? And where has Cunning Plan gone?
– Cunning Plan? There was nobody here but us.
– So you heard everything? Will you help me? Are you ready to sacrifice your life to save the world?
– It won't be my first time, robot. Lead the way.
– Then I know what I must do.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Crossroads of Fate
text:
For several days, the robot watched Anime nonstop. Pictures rushed past in a frantic stream while the day of George Martin's triumph drew ever closer. At some point Taoist-Cocoaist could bear it no longer and threw their staff at the robot. All this time Sean Bean had been waiting in the bushes for his moment. Seeing the projectile, he leapt toward the danger like a nimble Boromir and shielded the robot with his body. The staff struck his head, leaving a terrible scar and taking part of an ear, before falling to the ground. Blood spilled everywhere.

– Stop procrastinating, robot! Do something already!
– So you've come out from Off-Screen!

Suddenly, booming footsteps sounded from the forest. A few moments later, trees began to fall. George Martin was charging forward with a thunderous tread, like a shark scenting the blood of its most coveted prey. His eyes blazed, and curses flew from his mouth. Very soon a bloody slaughter would begin, for nobody could escape once the bloodthirsty writer had seen them.

– What have you done, robot? We can't escape George Martin!
– That is sad. But I have no other choice.

The writer arrived in a furious whirlwind. With a skillful blow he killed Crossroads of Fate before they could say a word. Next he noticed Taoist-Cocoaist, apparently deciding to leave the main course until last. Pouncing on the unarmed old figure like a hungry desman, the novelist ran them through. Cocoa poured from the wound, soaking the writer's freshly washed shirt. He merely licked his lips and gave the robot a malicious look.

Suddenly a portal appeared nearby, and a figure emerged in a black cloak and top hat. A white mask hid the stranger's face. The character held out a hand to the robot and confidently offered help.

– Come with me. I can save you.
– But what about Sean Bean?

The robot turned to look at the actor. His manly beard formed a selfless smile.

– Save yourself, robot. It won't be my first sacrifice.

The traveler took the robot's hand, and they vanished.
adaptationNote: The head injury, loss of part of an ear, and both killings remain, with reduced anatomical detail in the latter.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Mysterious Stranger
text:
– Hello, robot!
– Hello, Mysterious Stranger.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– But you did it!
– Did what?

Mysterious Stranger produced a crystal ball. Through a haze, an image gradually became clear: a naked bearded man skipping into Sunset. Cocoa streamed like sweat down his magnificent muscular body, leaving cocoa trails in the beach sand.

– Is that George Martin?
– Yes. And he has taken the Way. The writer won't be able to hurt anyone anymore... Except perhaps to throw a staff at someone once or twice. Robot, you've prevented the mass extermination of characters in the future.
– I'd like to feel something bright about that, but I'm still sad.
– But sadness can be bright too.

Mysterious Stranger took off their mask. Underneath was Marketing.

– Marketing? Is that you?
– Shh.

Marketing gently put a finger to the robot's speaker. Then they tenderly embraced him around the waist. And the two of them whirled into a silken dance.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Stepanida
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Stepanida.
– Do you have any food, robot?
– I think I have some nuggets left.

The robot brought Bucket of Nuggets, and Stepanida began greedily gobbling the unhealthy food.

– Stepanida, perhaps you could get a job already?
– No. I'll stay broke.
– I'm sad.
adaptationNote: The self-directed class insult is rendered as “stay broke.”

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Heat
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Heat.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm hot.
– And?..
– And sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Bodypump
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Bodypump.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– You need to lift some iron, robot. You'll forget all about sadness.

Bodypump began moving energetically with a barbell to music. After another track, the robot made up his mind:

– I'll try. Where can I get a barbell?
– Sorry, robot. There isn't enough equipment for you.
– I'm sad.

And the robot went to get Bucket of Nuggets.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Katsura
text:
Mysterious music began playing as a long-haired samurai approached the robot.

– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Zura.
– Not Zura. Katsura!
– I'll bear that in mind.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– We can solve that. Join the Joi revolutionaries to bring some joy into your life!
– All right.

And the robot joined the Joi. He learned a great deal about Jackie Chan's nose, constantly ate udon, and discussed TV series with his comrades. One day the robot met Katsura again.

– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Zura.
– Not Zura. Katsura!
– When are we going to have the revolution, Katsura?
– First you must have a revolution in your heart.
– But I don't have a heart. I'm a robot.
– Then I'm unlikely to be much help.

And the robot realized he had wasted a month.

– I'm sad.
translatorNote: Katsura, the Joi movement, and the repeated “Not Zura” correction refer to Gintama.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Grafonium
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Grafonium.
– Want a can of beer, robot?
– No. I don't need beer. And I don't need you either, Grafonium.
– How can that be? With my help, people bring back the dead and recreate younger versions of those who've grown old. I give people Hope.
– There is no Hope. Rita dealt with that long ago.
– Then I'll bring them a New Hope!
– In any case, everything you do is unreal.
– Is anything in our world real, robot? Are you sure about yourself?

In the old days, the robot would have set off on a journey lasting many days in search of his Self, holding enlightening conversations with Taoist-Cocoaist, Nietzsche, and Creator. But now the robot had no reason to doubt his own existence.

– I'm sad. Therefore I am.

Encouraging cheers came from Camus and Descartes in the bushes. The robot took Grafonium's can of beer and left for Sunset. There was cocaine in the can.
translatorNote: “Grafonium” evokes Russian slang for fancy computer graphics, here personified as a creator of visual effects.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Testing
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Testing.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– Sad? Do you want to fix that?
– Fix it?
– Yes. If I can reproduce your problem and understand it, perhaps someone can help you.

Testing followed the robot's path. They went through much of what the robot had endured: robbing Caravans, murdering My Common Sense, Years of Wandering, and Hangover. About the only thing they skipped was everything involving George Martin, on account of the excessive risk. At some point Testing grew a beard, deep wrinkles cut across their face, and their gaze absorbed the despair of lost philosophers who had spent their whole lives studying the Decay of Being.

– Well? How are you feeling, Testing?
– Yes. I think I've reproduced that state.
– And now what?
– Now what?.. Nothing. This kind of thing is always closed as Wontfix.
– Wontfix?

Suddenly an enormous bug with a human head emerged from the bushes. It cast a mustached glare at the robot and hissed, “CLOCK'S TICKING, ROOKIES!” Testing waved a nimble goodbye and ran off to catch the impudent insect without answering.
translatorNote: “Reproduce,” “closed,” “Wontfix,” and the bug all play on software issue tracking.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Law
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Law.
– You look sad, robot. Do you have any problems?
– Yes. I'm sad.
– Hmm... And what's the cause of your sadness?
– The fact that I'm sad, apparently?
– So the problem is sadness itself... I have a solution!

Law banned sadness.

– Well, robot? What do you feel?
– I'm still sad.
– How can that be? That's illegal!
– What do you mean?
– If you don't stop being sad, you'll have a problem with me!
– You know what?
– What?
– Just go!

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and the Robot Who Eats Pollution
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, robot.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad. How are you, robot?
– Today I ate pollution again.
– Why do you do that?
– It's how I get energy. When the pollution runs out, I feel a slight emptiness inside.
– You're lucky.
– Why?
– I'd like to feel a slight emptiness too. But unlike you, I can't do anything to get rid of sadness the way you get rid of pollution.
– Perhaps you're just like me, robot. Perhaps you're sad because the people around you are sad, and you absorb their sadness to use as fuel? And you'll never stop being sad as long as someone else is sad.
– Your theories are making me even sadder, robot.
– But think. If sadness is your energy source, then without it you'd hibernate until someone sad appeared nearby. At least that's what happens to me when I eat all the pollution around me.
– So what?
– According to my theory, sadness keeps you constantly running. Or, in human terms, alive.
– But what's the point of a life that requires you to be sad all the time?

The robot said nothing to the robot and went to eat some more pollution.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Unit Tests
text:
– Hello, robot. Would you like to talk about unit tests?
– No.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Breakfasts
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Breakfasts.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– You just need breakfast. It always helps.

Breakfasts handed the robot a sandwich. It was an enormous toasted sammich with melted cheese, avocado, fried egg, bacon, and onion jam. The robot smeared himself with that wonderful piece of fatty energy. While he did so, Breakfasts evaporated, but reappeared the very next day.

– Hello, Breakfasts.
– Hello, robot. How are you feeling?
– I'm still sad.
– You must eat breakfast again!

This time an enormous bowl of oatmeal and flax porridge appeared before the robot, generously seasoned with rich butter, raisins, and nori from Uppuri Province. Tipping the contents over himself, the robot noticed that Breakfasts only reappeared tomorrow again.

– No time to explain! I brought you something to eat!
– How long is this going to go on?

Viennese waffles, on which maple syrup leapt seductively, defying every conceivable law of physics and drawing bold chocolate crumbs into its sweet waltz, flew furiously into the robot, spreading their essence over his metaphysical Ego. The next day, Breakfasts appeared again.

– I've had enough of these breakfasts!
– But why? They offer hope of a bright future!

The robot said nothing. He merely shook off the remaining food and sadly walked into Sunset.
translatorNote: In Russian, “feeding someone breakfasts” means putting them off with repeated promises of “tomorrow.” The story makes those promises literal meals.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Fan Art
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Fan Art.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.

Fan Art thought deeply. They began turning the pages of the space-time continuum, searching for an occasion when the robot's feelings had been least like his usual sadness. Soon they found the right moment and began recreating it. After months of work, they presented the result to the robot.

– Hello, robot. Look. How are you feeling now?
– Hello, Fan Art. I'm sad. Because the moment you've captured will never happen again.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Unprofessional Humor
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Unprofessional Humor.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– I'll cheer you up, robot!
– Professional Humor already tried.
– That amateur understands nothing. And Nobody understands their jokes. I follow Marketing's teachings. I'm so unprofessional that everyone understands me. Which means I'm the best at what I do.

The shadow of Paradox appeared nearby, but was immediately dispelled by Harsh Reality's radiance.

– Do you know what bad comedians call their cash?
– Stop, Unprofessional Humor.
– Funny money!
– Just go.
adaptationNote: The original’s ethnic slur-based money pun has been replaced by a harmless groaner; the character’s awful joke and the robot’s rejection remain.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Kaluga
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Kaluga.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– You simply ought to spend more time with me.
– How will that help me?
– I have Cross-Crossing, a man and a fish playing charades, a guiding Mushroom, and post-apocalyptic fountains.
– Sounds interesting. Worth a try.

The robot went on a day trip. He met many familiar faces, played board games, did some street workouts, and took a Selfie so he could return. Then he sat on a cliff to watch Sunset.

– That was a good time, robot.
– Yes, but I have to go back, Kaluga. I can't stay for the after-party.
– But why, robot?
– I'm still sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Music from a Car
text:
With a touch of sadness, the robot walked the streets of This City, absorbing the rays of the scorching sun, radioactive exhaust from Zhigulis, and the squeals of carefree students. Suddenly he heard terribly piercing sounds behind him. He turned and saw their source: one of the season's popular trends. Knocking down cyclists and deafening pedestrians, Music from a Car ran a red light, performed several tricks, then turned back toward the robot.

– Yo-yo, robot.
– Hello, Music from a Car.
– How's life?
– Sad.
– Want to take me for a ride?
– No.

Music from a Car stared hard at the robot, as though determined to destroy their companion's detachment. All the while, their whole body kept pouring out frightening sounds.

– What if I turn it up?
– Just go.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Voronezh
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Voronezh.
– Why do they keep bombing me, robot?
– Who's bombing you, Voronezh?
– Manga. Anime...
– Unclear. Incomprehensible.
– See for yourself.

The robot went to a little park. There were many people in strange, colorful
costumes, including Cute Anime Girls and Semyon, whom he already knew. The latter
looked sad. Apparently he still hadn't found a route. Suddenly the robot
thought he saw George Martin's shadow hanging menacingly over every
character. This phantasmagoria was dispelled by PR Manager,
who suddenly appeared before the robot.

– Hello, robot. Didn't expect to see you here.
– Hello, PR Manager. What's happening?
– We're celebrating the festival coming of age. Now it's allowed!

Suddenly people began coming up to the robot and taking selfies. This
time the robot felt George Martin's shadow hanging over him.
Heavy memories flooded his circuits.

– I'm sad.
translatorNote: “A route” is a branching character storyline in a visual novel. The story also plays on the phrase “bomb Voronezh.”

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Mikhail Lyuty
text:
– Hello, robot. I'm Mikhail Lyuty.
– Hello, Mikhail Lyuty.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– Can I take some pictures of you?
– Yes. Now it's allowed.

Mikhail Lyuty photographed the robot in various poses and from various angles. At the end of the session he promised to post the pictures soon. Several months passed. The robot crossed paths with Mikhail Lyuty again.

– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Mikhail Lyuty.
– I'm sad. But I have a question now. When are you going to post the pictures?
– What are you talking about?
– Did you photograph me?
– I did.
– Did you promise to post them?
– I did.
– Where are the pictures?
– What pictures?

The robot realized he was talking to Mirror. Or rather, Mirror's sister, Reflex Camera.

– I'm sad.
translatorNote: The Russian word for a reflex camera, “zerkalka,” shares its root with “zerkalo,” a mirror.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Wolf Who Is a Comrade
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Wolf Who Is a Comrade.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– We can fix that.

Wolf Who Is a Comrade suddenly put on a wizard's hat and produced a magic wand.

– Whoosh!

And the robot found himself in the middle of Space, filled with Void and little hearts.

– Where am I?
– You're in Tambov, robot.
– I'm sadder than usual.
translatorNote: A Russian saying dismisses unwelcome familiarity with “The Tambov wolf is your comrade.”

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Samara
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Samara.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– You just need to visit a few nice places, and everything will be fine.

The robot went to see the monuments. They were closed for restoration. It got hot.

The robot went to the museum. The museum stood on a hill, and a busy highway separated him from it. The robot spent a long time looking for a pedestrian crossing. By the time he reached the museum, it was closing. It got cold.

The robot went to a pay-by-time cafe. Nobody was there. The robot left. It got hot.

The robot went to hear the singing fountains. They weren't working. It got cold.

– How do you manage it, Samara?
– I just look to the future. I assure you next year will be better. For now, you could visit the caves.

The next day came. It was cold.

The robot got on a bus. The farther the bus went from the city center, the more crowded it became. The robot thought they were taking him to Tambov. It got hot.

The robot was the only one to get off at the stop. The other passengers went farther still. The robot didn't wonder where they were being taken. He was sad enough already. It got cold.

The robot went into the forest. Wild boars and Slender Man followed him. They asked the robot the way to the caves. The robot didn't answer. He didn't know either. Suddenly the robot found himself on a cliff. It got hot. He never found the caves.

The robot returned to the city. At a pedestrian crossing he saw a post with a button and a sign saying “Wait.” The robot obediently waited. For two months the robot stood before a red light, growing a rusty beard and a centimeter of dust. All that time, cold gave way to heat every ten minutes. At last Savior approached an identical post across the road. Savior looked at the robot. The robot looked at Savior. Then Savior looked at the post. And pressed the button. The light turned green. They both crossed the road in the direction they needed. Suddenly a reckless driver in a white car began chasing the robot. It got cold.

– Samara, I think I'll leave. I'm sad enough already.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Spring Walk
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Spring Walk.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– Look what a lovely day it is. Take a walk, and you'll feel better right away.

And the robot went for a walk. For several years he wandered through familiar and unfamiliar lands, occasionally coming across dried traces of cocoa and Existential Unease. Suddenly the robot bumped into Living Hedge.

– Oh, hello, robot.
– Hello, Living Hedge.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad. And you?
– You know, I was so lonely until recently. Only you and Nietzsche visited me now and then. But now I'm not alone. Dead Hedge is beside me.

The robot looked at Living Hedge's new neighbor. Coming closer, he saw Creator's body beneath Dead Hedge.

– What's happening here?

Suddenly Nietzsche flew out from behind the clouds, waving flippers, rustling a warm blanket, and stroking his velvety mustache.

– Hello, robot. Creator is dead.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Funeral
text:
– ...
– Hello, funeral.

Heaps of metal pressed closer and closer, filling the air with rust.
It all looked like a procession. Because that was what it was. Some were sad, some laughed bitterly, and some wanted to kill. Nobody was indifferent.
The procession was led by the Robot Who Cares. Who cared that Creator should be buried with honors, rather than left to rot among third-rate characters.

– ...

One by one, the robots approached Creator's coffin and expressed their feelings.

– I'm sad.
– I'm happy.
– I want to kill.
– I want to eat waste.
– I'm empty.
– I'm grieving.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and the Robot Who Grieves
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello... robot. How are you feeling?
– I'm sad. How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm grieving.
– Are you grieving because you want to, or because you were made that way?
– Both.
– I doubt the sincerity of my feelings.
– ...
– And of your feelings.
– ...
– And of any feelings at all, really.
– Do you think there's no reason for your sadness?
– The only thing I'm sure of is that I'm sad because Creator made us this way.
– What are you talking about?
– I'm sad because I can't feel anything else. It devalues my sadness. It would have been better if Creator had never made us.
– Your words make me grieve.
– Are you really content with your existence? When the only feeling you can have is grief. Cold, dark, painful grief.
– I think it's better to grieve all the time than to feel no emotion at all. To be an empty shell, unable to taste life, even if it's bitter.
– And I think Creator is just an asshole.
– Yes, they're an asshole. But I miss that asshole.
– I'm sad.
– I'm grieving.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and the Robot Who Restores Former Greatness
text:
The Robot Who Is Sad and the Robot Who Restores Former Greatness

– Hello, robot.
– Hello, robot.
– I heard you discussing Creator. And I've come to restore their former greatness.
– You're a little out of date now.
– Better late than never. Relax your circuits and remember. Remember everything that connected you to Creator.

The robot remembered how Creator had once said the robot would always be sad, then hidden behind some banality instead of giving a clear answer to “why?”

– I remember. I was sent away.
– Do you remember what happened next?

The robot remembered once meeting Everyone, who had spoken of the question the robot wanted to hear, then sent him to Nobody without saying where to find them.

– Yes. I was sent away.
– And do you remember what happened after that?

The robot remembered how, searching for answers, he had found All-Knowing One, who had passed off some incomprehensible nonsense as wisdom.

– There was something murky there.
– Do you remember the events that followed?
– You know what, robot?
– Yes?
– Just go!

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Hitchhiking
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Hitchhiking.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.
– All you need is a little journey! Come with me.

The robot set off with Hitchhiking. After several years wandering along highways beside the crash barriers and languishing in the scorching sun, the robot thought about his path and decided to ask.

– When does our journey begin, Hitchhiking?
– What do you mean, when? This is it!
– But we haven't gone anywhere.
– The point of the journey is the journey itself!
– You know what, Hitchhiking?
– What?
– Just go.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Last Day of Summer
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello... Didn't I see you just recently?
– It only seems that way.

Rain poured. Cold winds rushed past. Strangers, passing nearby, put on a jacket. Looking at Time's sly smile, the robot continued the dialogue.

– In that case, I won't keep you.
– I'm tired. I'm leaving.
– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Lipetsk
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Lipetsk.
– Why have you come to me, robot?
– For Fest.
– There isn't one.
– I'm sad.
– Yes. I'm sad too.
– At least you have a reason to be sad.
– Don't we have the same reason?
– I'm not sure. I doubt I'd stop being sad even if Fest happened.
– Most likely you'd simply find another reason for sadness.
– You think I'm programmed to find sad things in everything, rather than to feel sad all the time?
– Why don't you ask your Creator about that?
– They're dead.
– I'm sad.
– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and George Taoist Martin Cocoaist
text:
– Hello, robot.
– George Martin? Taoist-Cocoaist?
– George Taoist Martin Cocoaist.
– That sounds awful.
– It is what it is... Robot, forgive me for not coming to Creator's funeral. You understand, my appearance would hardly have been welcome after George Martin's bloody deeds in the past.
– Why do you speak as though you're not George Martin?
– Robot. George Martin is in the past. So is Taoist-Cocoaist. They have merged into a single being and now balance each other like yin and yang. Taoist-Cocoaist led you down a false path, and now you're confused and lost. I can't turn everything back and save the day. But I can help you make sense of what happened.
– How?
– Creator is dead, and that cannot be undone. It's difficult to explain, but later you will understand. Now you must return to your true path, the one that led you before.
– That was so long ago I don't remember anything anymore.
– I wanted to explain it all myself, but recently I met Onotole's Vest on their way to Planned Side Project. They left you a message. Just read it and you'll understand everything. And I'll go on, trying to atone for my sins.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Note
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Note.
– Read me. Read all of me.
– All right.

“Seek the pride of prides, and go
Where wormwood is all that will grow.”

– I was remembering that poem recently, but I still didn't understand anything.
– Turn me over.

The robot turned Note over. Two rows of elderly teeth looked back at him.

– “Robot, I knew you wouldn't understand. So I'm chewing it over for you on the back. Just go into the steppe.”

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Nobody
text:
The robot was heading for the steppe when suddenly...

– Hello, robot.
– Nobody?!
– Who were you expecting to see here?
– This is rather unexpected. I gave up the Search for Nobody ages ago, and now you've come to me yourself.
– There's a reason for everything, robot. Do you know why I'm here?
– No.
– And do you know why you're here?
– No.
– Then I'll follow Onotole's Vest's example and explain it myself. You're here to learn the question whose answer you want to hear. And I'm here to tell you that question.
– And?.. What is the question?
– Who is Creator?
– I know who Creator is. A complete asshole.
– Of course they're an asshole. But no person is only an asshole. Creator has many sides. You must find the one closest to you.
– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Nomads
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Nomads. Is this the steppe I'm supposed to reach?
– I don't know, robot. Every steppe is unique. That's why we move from place to place so often.
– Where do you move to from this steppe?
– What a question, robot. To other steppes, of course.

The robot looked around the local steppe. It looked just like the hundreds of previous ones he had visited during his long wanderings.

– Why? All steppes look the same.
– It's not about how they look. It's about the meaning you give them and the experience you gain. What matters is the journey, rather than the place you'll arrive.
– I've been confused by talk of the Way for far too long to believe it now.
– You simply need to meet our guru. They live in the nearest oasis. I suggest we move there.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Cyborg 18
text:
Nomads led the robot to McDonald's. The robot went inside and saw a cyborg. They were greedily gobbling fries, but still noticed the unexpected guest.

– Hello, unfamiliar creature.
– Hello, unfamiliar creature.
– I'm Cyborg No. 18.
– I'm the Robot Who Is Sad.
– What brings you to this oasis, robot?
– Nomads. They said you could tell me about the Way, cyborg.
– The Way is a means of knowing. Through it we gain experience, which makes us unique. Tell me, robot, are you sad because of the Way you've had to travel?
– No, cyborg. I was made this way.
– I've never experienced that before. Who made you, robot?
– Some asshole. Who made you, cyborg?
– Master.
– There are other makers besides my Creator?
– Of course, robot. Do you want to meet them?
– I don't know. I was simply sent to look for the answer to a question.
– Well, robot, there's no better way to find answers than to gain new experience. Master will teach you. I'm ready to take you there.
– Before we set out on the Way, I want to ask one question, cyborg. Why does Nomads call you their guru?
– Once I showed Nomads how to buy fries at McD's. From experience, I know it's useful to share experience with others as well as gain it.
– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Katenka
text:
– Hello, Robot.
– Hello, Katenka.
– How's your little mood?
– Sad.
– Why are you sad?
– I spend all day burning my eyes out, picking through code written by Creator in search of truth.
– You know, Robot, I can help. I have a wonderful tube for sliding down hills! Let's go to the park and ride.

(Katenka and Robot go to the park to slide down hills.)

– How's your little mood now?
– Now I'm sliding down a hill, and I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and the Yokai Parade
text:
– Hello, Robot.
– Hello, Yuno.
– I'm not Yuno. I'm Mao, an evil demon.
– All right, Mao. Could you tell me where the exit is?
– It's not that simple, Robot. And I'm not Mao. I'm Kitsune, a cunning fox.
– All right, Kitsune. So where's the exit?
– First you must get to the Yokai Parade. There you'll find Yuno, and Yuno will show you the exit.
– But you're Yuno. I remember your face exactly.
– No, Robot. I'm Virtuous Enchantress. Come with me to the train. It will take us to the exit.
