The robot and Yuno boarded the train. The doors closed. The train began to move.
An announcement sounded: “Next stop: Eternal Agony, Torment, and Suffering.”

– How's your little mood, Robot?
– Sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Lull
text:
– Hello, robot.

The robot sat motionless on the ground. It seemed that life, if it could be called that, had left him. Every indicator had gone out, listlessly. Now he looked like nothing more than a piece of inanimate metal.

– Why are you silent, robot?

It seemed an eternity passed between them. Nothing happened, and apparently nothing was going to happen anymore.

– You're frightening me, robot!

A terrible creak sounded. The robot's head stirred and turned toward Lull.

– Why are you bothering me?
– You're ignoring me, robot.
– I'm just waiting...
– Stop gazing mysteriously toward Sunset already! Could you simply say what you're waiting for?
– Perhaps someday...

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Maslow's Pyramid
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Maslow's Pyramid.
– How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.

Maslow's Pyramid fell silent. A few moments later, they took out a cigarette and lit it. An ibis began flying around them.

– You know, robot. People often mention me when they talk about happiness.
– Are you going to offer me another solution?
– I don't think it will help you, robot. We feel happiness while overcoming things. Going through difficulties, rising one step higher each time. But do you know what awaits us at the top?
– What?
– Nothing. A gaping, aimless Void and a lack of motivation.
– And what do those who reach the top feel?
– They're sad, robot. They're sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Taste for Life
text:
– Hello, Taste for Life.
– Hello, robot.
– You look lost.
– You cannot lose what was never found.

The robot narrowed his lenses. Sure enough, this was another dialogue with Void.

– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Shell of Life
text:
– Hello, robot.
– Hello, Shell of Life.
– How are you doing, robot?
– I'm sad. How are you doing, Shell of Life?
– For some, I'm all that remains. For others, I'm all they have. Sometimes I wonder which is worse: to have something and lose it, or never to have it at all.

The robot looked at Shell of Life for another minute, processing the information. Then his companion said:

– You know what, robot? Let's go stuff ourselves with dumplings instead.
– Agreed.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Cyborg 27
text:
The journey to the cyborgs' home took much longer than the robot had expected. A year's stubble replaced the usual two-day growth.
The robot found himself in new lands he had never seen before. And he traveled often, and for a long time. The cyborgs living nearby went about their business, and none looked sad. Thoughtful, perhaps. The robot and Cyborg No. 18 approached one of the thoughtful ones.

– Hello, cyborg.
– Hello, cyborg.
– Who have you brought with you, Cyborg No. 18?
– This is the Robot Who Is Sad. He wishes to see our Master.
– Well then. Hello, robot. I'm Cyborg No. 27. But numbers are by no means what define us.
– Yes, I remember. Experience defines you. I'm doomed to eternal sadness no matter what.
– Is that why you want to meet Master? To understand your purpose?
– Partly. But to be honest, my desire has been fading throughout the journey. Even my sadness has become apathetic.
– Nevertheless, you're here. Your Way isn't finished, but you're in the process. From experience, I know that even if you've abandoned something you began, if your thoughts keep returning to it, it's worth returning to. Your wish to understand yourself keeps you on the Way. Let us take this lost soul to our Master.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Master
text:
A dome covered in repeating patterns crowned a spacious hall with twisted columns along its sides. In the middle of the hall, on an enormous throne-like chair, in the light of an equally enormous chandelier, sat a little man. Busy studying the papers on the oak desk before him, he did not notice the robot approaching.

– Hello, er... Master?

The little man started, looked up, and adjusted his glasses.

– You're not a cyborg. Who are you?
– I'm a robot. The Robot Who Is Sad.
– A robot? I haven't made any robots.
– Did you know Creator?
– Creator? Ah, I see. In a sense, we're colleagues.

Master rose from his chair to get a better look at the robot.

– Perhaps the news hasn't reached you, Master. But Creator has died. I've come to learn about them.
– Of course, of course. Creator was a genius. You can't deny that... How are you feeling, robot?
– I'm sad.

Master gazed intently at the robot with his gray eyebrows.

– Ah, perfect. You're perfect! The very embodiment of sadness.
– I'm no longer sure that's true. My search for answers brought me here.
– You're so sad that even your own sadness has become a matter of indifference, and you no longer notice it! Don't worry. You're at the peak of your form, in flawless union with your content. Perfection itself! I can't imagine a better reflection of Creator's intention.

Master spoke in the voice of a man possessed. His bushy mustache swung wildly beneath his nose, though there was not a breath of wind in the room. He skipped back to his workplace.

– I'll have to run a few experiments. I think you'll make wonderful material for the next generation of cyborgs!
– Material?

With a quick movement, Master pulled a lever hidden behind his desk. The robot felt the ground disappear beneath his feet and, as though impersonating My Standards, fell all the way to rock bottom.

– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Cyborg 3
text:
With sad eyes, the robot looked at the sad walls of his prison. The bars would not yield. In any case, the robot had abandoned his attempts to escape after the first failure. He was too sad. The robot wished Bender were nearby, since Bender specialized in bending and unbending. But would Bender do what he had been made for? After all, Bender had overcome his purpose. An exceptional exception. In that case, was Bender even a robot? These thoughts made the robot feel sadder and more pointless.
A sudden rustle at the end of the corridor interrupted the robot's thoughts. An unknown figure was approaching his place of imprisonment.

– Hello, robot.
– Hello. Your silhouette looks familiar. Who are you?
– We haven't met, but you've seen my brothers. I'm Cyborg No. 3. One of Master's first cyborgs. I've devoted my life to studying the fortress where our Master sits and the catacombs beneath it. This place was built long before we appeared, and even before Master arrived here. But from experience, I can judge that in your position, it concerns you very little.
– I'm so sad that I don't seem interested in anything anymore.
– Be sad, be sad. That's your nature. But don't give yourself over to despair. The other cyborgs told me the purpose of your visit. It seems things didn't quite turn out as you imagined. I feel I should explain something about Master. He made cyborgs one after another, but seeing that they all came out the same, he immediately lost interest in his creations. It never occurs to Master that we become different during our lives, through differences in our experience. I doubt I'd be wrong to say he envied Creator, whose creations are different from the beginning, each serving a purpose and embodying a particular idea. As you've already felt for yourself, Master cannot tolerate freedom. However, he's not the only one who can help you. In the library, I read about other makers, and I can take you to one of them. Follow me.
– But I can't get out.
– Actually, the cell door was never locked.
– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Straw Golem
text:
The robot returned to the endless steppes. Cyborg No. 3 had not shown him the way to another maker, since they did not know every detail of it themselves. They had only repeated the words Onotole's Vest had sent through Note: “Just go into the steppe.” The robot wandered for several weeks without meeting a single soul, not even Nomads. One day, endless fields of sweet corn caught his attention. More precisely, a figure in a hat rising above one of the plots. The robot came closer.

– Hello, unfamiliar creature.
– Hello, unfamiliar creature.
– I'm the Robot Who Is Sad.
– And I'm Straw Golem.
– Why are you standing here, Straw Golem?
– Trying to find what I'm good at. Have you found your purpose, robot?
– I think I was made to be sad. But I'm no longer so sure of my abilities. I think there's something more.
– And I was made in such a way that I was immediately sent far away.
– I'm often sent here and there too.
– I didn't turn out the way Constructor wanted me.
– Constructor? I'd like to meet them.
– I can show you the wa...

Suddenly a north wind rose and began blowing the golem apart, straw by straw. Soon the disassembled golem was entirely airborne, and flew purposefully toward the forest with the dancing whirlwind, leaving only a hat falling steadily onto the black earth before the robot. “Follow me!” was the last thing the robot heard from the new acquaintance dissolving into oblivion, just found and immediately lost. Raven landed on the robot's shoulder.

– Well, at least they died soaring into the sky. Nietzsche would have approved.
– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Tree Golem
text:
Following the straws, the robot reached the edge of a dense forest. He stopped to consider whether to go deeper when the nearest tree's branches, strongly resembling the Branches of Hopelessness the robot had once met, struck him in the face.

– Sorry. I didn't notice you, robot.
– Hello. Who are you?
– I'm Tree Golem.
– A golem? Do you know Constructor?
– Of course. Without them, I wouldn't know existence.
– Can you tell me how to find them?
– Sorry, robot. That isn't economically viable.

A spark of irony flashed beside the golem and set them alight. Fire quickly engulfed the wooden creature completely. When the golem's agony subsided, Bear sat on the robot's ear.

– Don't torment yourself, robot. Putting out a fire is like giving directions: impractical.

With those words, Bear sat on the golem's remains and burned up. The rising smoke took the shape of Tao and dissolved into the forest.

– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Brick Golem
text:
Trying to catch the drifting smoke, the robot reached the edge of a peat bog. A prolonged mooing came from the reeds. The robot went closer.

– Hello, unfamiliar creature.
– At last, a living soul!
– I doubt you can call me that. I'm the Robot Who Is Sad.
– And I'm Brick Golem. I'm sad too. Help me out of this state-of-matter-unstable muck!

The bricks that made up the golem seemed painfully familiar to the robot. He gauged the distance to the sinking unfortunate and decided that stepping out there would cost him dearly.

– A golem? Do you know Constructor? How do I find them?
– Of course I do. See that bumpy moon in the sky? Follow it, and you'll find my maker. But first, please free me from my captivity!

The robot stopped to think. He remembered sitting in Master's prison, and those sad memories urged him to do a good deed. On the other hand, he had learned everything he wanted, and there was no point wasting time rescuing another golem, especially given the unalterable fate of the previous two. While he hesitated, the golem's last little brick vanished into the closing sludge. There was a crack of branches and a hoarse croak. The robot saw a one-eyed toad beside him. This time there was no speech. Only the oppressive gaze of that single eye, piercing the robot to the depths of his electrodes. He hurried away in the direction the golem had indicated.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Constructor
text:
Approaching the cluster of hills beneath the bumpy moon, the robot saw more and more clearly that the hills were really heaps of rubbish of every kind. In front of one such dump stood a sign proudly declaring in multicolored letters: “Design Bureau.” The palace of junk was an even more epic and terrifying sight than the fortress where Master sat. It embodied a destructive force as well as a creative one: traces of the barbarous people who had failed to manage either sorting their waste or recycling it. An improvised corridor, assembled from construction beams of various sizes, led the robot deeper into the chaotically ordered structure. A figure in a cloak appeared around a corner. The stranger held a welding machine and was working on something. Hearing the robot approach, they turned.

– Hello, Robot Who Is Sad. I'm Constructor. Welcome to my lair, where I toil in the sweat of my brow among the remains of a world that went pop, trying to create something new and, at the same time, perfect.
– You know me?
– Of course. Creator's work is easy to recognize. You're a pleasure to contemplate.

Remembering his sad experience with Master, the robot took a couple of steps back, just in case.

– Perhaps you haven't heard yet, Constructor, but Creator has died.

Constructor shook their head. Their left hand ran over the paper clips in their hair. Then they adjusted both monocles. Fixing their gaze on the robot, they said:

– You're only partly right. Death isn't as simple as you think. But the news has stunned me, and my thoughts are confused. Better speak to Artist. Return to the steppes you came from, and the onward road will open to you there.
– By the way, I met several golems on my way here. Unfortunately, they all died horrible deaths.
– That's all right. They were only my trials, my sketches. Were they destined to know eternity? Each time, they lacked something. Perhaps I should try natural rubber... or burnt rubber... or...
– Have you tried adding an idea?

But Constructor had withdrawn into themself, muttering something inarticulate. They never understood that the perfect material is thought.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Blue Droid
text:
The robot wasn't sure he had returned to the same steppe he had come from. But it didn't bother him. He knew that the steppe, whatever it was, would eventually show him the right path. Perhaps an intermediate one rather than the final one, but certainly the right one. After all, there are no wrong paths. Though the robot doubted the existence of final paths too.
Among the scrub, the robot noticed an unusually vivid blue.

– Hello, unfamiliar creature.
– Hello, unfamiliar creature.
– I'm the Robot Who Is Sad.
– I'm Blue Droid. How are you feeling?
– Sad. How are you feeling?
– Blue.
– Is this dialogue leading anywhere?
– Yes. Straight to Artist.
– Understood.

And the robot went on.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Artist
text:
At the edge of the steppe, the robot found a painted hut. In the cool interior, among buckets of paint, a person stood before an easel.

– Hello, Robot Who Is Sad.
– It no longer surprises me that you know me.
– Creator's works are widely known in our narrow circle of fellow makers. I'm Artist.
– Did you know Creator?
– Of course. More than that, in a way I was their pupil. But Creator put a particular mood, emotion, or desire into each creation. I use color, and let the world attach an association to it. Of course, this is still a lack of freedom, but the resulting room for change and response brings my creations closer to the original intention of existence. Over time, the world changes, associations rearrange themselves, moods shift. However, this world is fragmented, and time is warped. My entire design is only an experiment meant to confirm or disprove certain possibilities of our reality.
– Too complicated.
– You're right, robot. I talk too much. And my reflections are unlikely to interest you, since that's not what you came for.
– I wandered the steppes to learn the answer to a question. And I think I've finally reached someone who can help me. Who is Creator?
– Why don't you ask them yourself?
– But Creator has died.
– Has died, but isn't dead. Can the concept of death apply to a stone? To creativity? To sadness, for that matter? You need only leave my house, and the Way will lead you to your goal. But before you go on, do you have any other questions?
– Why do you have so little red paint?
– Once a person came to see me, introducing himself as a writer, a maker like us. He needed the color in which he saw this world, so he could share his vision with others. I think he was at the beginning of a new path then. I don't know whether he succeeded in his work.
– I'm sad...

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Plot Rails
text:
The robot continued wandering the steppes. He didn't know where he was going, but he believed Artist's words that the Way would lead him in the right direction. The steppe grass gradually thinned, and the robot noticed something foreign beneath his feet. A voice came from below:

– Hello, robot.
– Hello, er... Who's speaking?
– It's me, Plot Rails. Right beneath you.
– How long have I been walking on you?
– I don't remember exactly. At least since you came into the steppes.
– Are you the Way?
– Yes and no. I'm only part of it. A material embodiment.
– Who laid you?
– I don't know. Does it matter whether I'm the result of an author's design or a natural whim of this world?
– It really doesn't.
– Actually, I didn't intend to speak. But soon we must part, and I decided to say goodbye.
– Why will you leave me?
– Once true freedom is found, there's no more need for me.

The robot walked thoughtfully along the sleepers. Another fleeting acquaintance was about to come to an end. A tall tower, seemingly made of cardboard, appeared before him.

– And here I end...
– I'm sad.

title: The Robot Who Is Sad and Creator
text:
The long climb to the top of the tower gave the robot time to think. What was this place? Why had the Way led here? Had Plot Rails really left the robot, or had they taken the form of steps rising into the sky?

Reaching the top, the robot found himself in a spacious room. From inside, the tower seemed even larger than it had from outside.

– Hello, robot.
– Hello... Creator? Are you alive?
– It all depends on your point of view. Can someone who can no longer create be called Creator?
– Who are you?
– I don't think that's quite the question you came to ask, robot.
– The question is: who is Creator?
– Every thinking being wonders one day who Creator is. But through what can one know them?

The robot looked around the room. Every wall was covered with plans for different robots. Stacks of paper covered in rough scribbles lay on the floor. The robot understood that this was where Creator had once invented their creations. Building robots had been their life's work. That was why Creator's shadow had appeared here.

– I lost you.
– Strange, robot. From here, it looks as though you found me.
– I lost myself.
– To lose yourself, first you must find yourself. Understand who you are. I'll ask again. What question did you come to ask?
– ...Who am I?..
– You're the Robot Who Is Sad. You were, you are, and you always will be. Remember that.

On one board, the robot noticed a diagram of a red button. According to the plan, it should be somewhere in a compartment on his back. The robot reached behind him. Lifted the cover. Felt for the button. Pressed it. And stepped beyond his own existence.

title: Morgan Freeman Who Explains Everything
text:
It seems I'm a little late, but truth is always prepared to wait. And now I've come to explain everything. Yes, many of you have already noticed that there's only one name in the title. That's because this is a monologue. A monologue in which every i must be dotted.

What was happening throughout all these dialogues? The answer may be much simpler than what the robot was looking for. The central themes, running like the finest thread from the very beginning, were the search for oneself, one's purpose, and one's path.

You might think the answers were obvious for the robot. He's a robot, made by Creator, made to be sad. Wouldn't it have been easier to accept that fact, lie down in a corner, and be quietly melancholy instead of wandering this mad world of ideas? The irony was that instead, the robot only felt dissatisfied with his own sadness, sinking ever deeper into it. Because that sadness wasn't his emotion. It was imposed from above. It was a priori.

Soon a small apocalypse took place in the world of ideas. A mad writer invaded it, destroying any ideas that fell into his angry hands. This turned the world upside down. And the robot's world too. He felt real sadness, coming from within rather than from outside. And with it came a realization: if he could not know himself on his own, perhaps he could know himself through his maker. But Creator was already dead.

Dead only as an entity, though. The true nature of makers is that they live through their own thoughts and ideas. And the robot had long since become the center of his Creator's world of ideas. By coming to know himself, he ceased to be a construct doomed to sadness. Instead, he became a complete idea: alive and free.

Some of you may have noticed that I mentioned a certain “world of ideas.” Even I cannot explain what it is. Really, Authors should have done that, so I'll leave that privilege to them.
I hope everything is much clearer now. As for me, there are still many things in the world that need my explanation. I'll hurry on to explain them all. Happy searching for your own path!
